lead: When a model is trained it must work well on data it has never seen. Cross‑validation estimates that future performance and helps pick the best model among many. It is used before a final test on a hold‑out set, in competitions, and in industry pipelines such as predicting demand for UPI transactions or forecasting power load after a Chennai power cut.

blocks.text: The simplest split is train / validation / test. The training part fits the parameters. The validation part tunes hyper‑parameters. The test part gives the final unbiased estimate. Some syllabi call the validation set a "hold‑out" set.

items: Train set: used to learn model weights.
Validation set: used to choose λ, depth, etc.
Test set: never touched until the end.

blocks.text: k‑fold cross‑validation reduces variance of the validation estimate. The data are divided into k equal folds. Each fold becomes validation once while the other k‑1 folds form the training set. The metric is averaged over the k runs.

items: Shuffle the whole data set.
Split into k folds of equal size.
For i = 1 to k:
Train on all folds except i.
Validate on fold i and record the metric.
Average the k recorded metrics.
Leave‑one‑out CV is k‑fold with k = n (number of samples).
Stratified CV keeps class proportions in each fold for classification.

blocks.text: For regression the common metrics are RMSE and MAE.

blocks.where: e = predicted – actual; n = number of examples; Σ(e²) = sum of squared errors.

blocks.text: For classification the basic metrics are accuracy, precision, recall and F1‑score.

blocks.where: TP = true positives; TN = true negatives; FP = false positives; FN = false negatives.
Measures how many predicted positives are correct.
Measures how many actual positives are captured.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall.

blocks.text: Some syllabi label these as "evaluation metrics" and stress that the same metric must be used for all folds when comparing models.

Model selection means choosing the algorithm and its hyper‑parameters that give the lowest expected error on new data. The process is: define a search space, evaluate each candidate with cross‑validation, pick the best, then train on the full training set and finally test once.

items: List candidate models (e.g., linear, ridge, lasso).
Choose hyper‑parameter grid (e.g., λ = 0.1, 1, 10).
Run k‑fold CV for every candidate.
Record the average metric.
Select the candidate with the smallest error metric (e.g., RMSE, MAE) or the largest score metric (e.g., accuracy, F1).
Retrain on train + validation data.
Report performance on the untouched test set.
Using the test set to tune hyper‑parameters leaks information and gives an optimistic estimate.
Data leakage can also happen if preprocessing (scaling, imputation) is fitted on the whole data before splitting.
When the data are time‑ordered, use a forward‑chaining split instead of random k‑fold.

blocks.text: In some syllabi the term "model selection" is used interchangeably with "hyper‑parameter tuning". Both are part of the validation workflow described above.

examples.question: A data set contains 1000 house‑price records (price in ₹ thousand). You apply ridge regression with λ = 1 and use 5‑fold cross‑validation. The RMSE obtained on the five folds are 4.2, 4.5, 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4. Compute the average RMSE and state whether the model meets a target error of 5 ₹ thousand.
steps: Divide by the number of folds (5): 21.5 ÷ 5 = 4.3 ₹ thousand.
Compare 4.3 with the target 5 ₹ thousand. Since 4.3 ≤ 5, the model satisfies the requirement.
examples.answer: The average RMSE is 4.3 ₹ thousand, which meets the target of ≤ 5 ₹ thousand.

traps: Using the test set to choose λ gives an overly optimistic RMSE; the test data must stay unseen until the final evaluation.
Confusing MAE with RMSE: MAE does not square errors, so its scale is different and cannot be compared directly to RMSE values.
When computing precision and recall, swapping TP with FP changes the numbers dramatically; always read the definition carefully.
In leave‑one‑out CV, the computation time grows proportionally to n times the cost of training a model, which can become very high for large n.

quiz.q: What does the acronym CV stand for in model evaluation?
Explain why the average of k‑fold RMSE values is a better estimate of test error than a single train‑validation split.
quiz.a: A single split may be lucky or unlucky depending on how the data are partitioned, leading to high variance. Averaging over k different partitions reduces this variance and gives a more stable estimate of how the model will perform on unseen data.

quiz.q: Given TP=40, FP=10, FN=5, TN=45, compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
A practitioner reports an RMSE of 3.2 from 10‑fold CV but later says the same model achieved an RMSE of 2.9 on the test set. What could explain this discrepancy?
quiz.a: Possible reasons: (1) data leakage during CV (e.g., scaling on full data); (2) the test set is not representative (easier examples); (3) random chance due to small test size; (4) the model was retrained on more data after CV, improving performance.
MAE = Σ|e| ÷ n, where e = predicted – actual.

quiz.q: You have five RMSE values: 5.0, 4.8, 5.2, 4.9, 5.1. Compute the average RMSE and state if it meets a target of 5.0.
quiz.a: Sum = 25.0, average = 25.0/5 = 5.0. The average meets the target exactly.

quiz.q: Why is stratified k‑fold used for classification problems with imbalanced classes?
quiz.a: Stratified k‑fold keeps the proportion of each class in every fold similar to the whole data set, preventing some folds from having too few minority class examples, which would make the validation metric unreliable.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, cross‑validation is combined with automated pipelines (e.g., MLflow) to track experiments. Research explores nested CV for unbiased model selection and Bayesian optimization to replace grid search. Future study may cover time‑series CV, Monte‑Carlo CV, and how deep‑learning frameworks implement validation loops.
